title: Detection of Domains
summary: This strategy detects adversary domain acquisition for malicious use, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (Acquire Infrastructure: Domains). Adversaries register lookalike domains, aged typosquats, and throwaway hosts so that phishing links, payload delivery, and command and control survive basic blocking. Because the registration happens at a registrar with no relationship to you, detection is external: newly registered domain feeds filtered for names that resemble your brand, certificate transparency monitoring, passive domain name system records, registration and name server history, and the point where your users actually resolve or click the domain. The most actionable internal signal is a client resolving a lookalike name that has never been seen in your environment, especially from an email client. The strategy fails when it depends only on a blocklist, because new domains appear faster than curation, and when it matches too loosely on brand text, which floods the queue with unrelated names that merely share a syllable.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for internet domain names that attackers register in order to imitate your company. A domain name is the address people type, such as example.com. Attackers buy names that look almost the same as yours, then use them in fake links.
beginner.whyItMatters: A well chosen lookalike name is hard for a person to spot in a hurry. It also survives many email filters, because the domain itself is new rather than known bad. If you do not watch new registrations that mention your brand, your first warning may be an employee entering a password on a fake page. Finding it early allows you to block the name and start the removal process.
howItWorks: An external feed lists domain names registered in the last few days, with the registrar and name servers.
The detection matches those names against your brand, product names, and common typing mistakes.
It also watches certificate records, because a new site usually gets a certificate before it is used.
If a lookalike name is found, it is pushed into blocking tools before users see it.
Internal resolver and proxy logs show whether anyone in your network has already visited the name.
The analyst scores the case by brand similarity, first contact, and whether credentials were entered.
beginner.example: Think of a shop that finds a van painted in its colours, parked outside its own door, with a driver taking payments. The van is not on any company list, and it appeared this morning. You would radio the manager rather than wait for a customer to complain. New lookalike domains are the van.
takeaways: Lookalike domains are new, so known bad lists will not contain them yet.
Compare new registrations with your brand and typical typing mistakes, not with all new names.
Check whether anyone in your network already resolved the name, because that turns a lead into a case.

objectives: Explain how lookalike and typosquat domains support phishing and payload delivery
Identify external feeds and internal logs that reveal malicious domain acquisition early
Build a brand similarity match that controls false positives from unrelated names
Correlate a new registration with internal resolution and click data to prioritise the case
Describe a block, warn, and takedown workflow for a confirmed malicious domain
dataSources: Newly registered domain feeds with registration date, registrar, and name server records
Certificate transparency monitoring alerts for newly issued certificates containing your brand or product names
DNS resolver logs with queried name, client address, and first seen timestamp for each name
Web proxy logs showing the request path, user agent, and submitted form data for newly observed domains
Phishing report mailboxes and user reported messages that contain links to external domains
logic: The pattern is a domain registered recently whose name is closely similar to your brand, product, or executive names, appearing in external registration or certificate data, and then appearing in resolution or proxy logs inside your network. The fields to correlate are the registered name, the registration date, the name server records, the certificate subject, the internal client that resolved the name, and the request or email that carried the link. The benign version is a partner, franchisee, or marketing campaign domain that carries your name with permission and a stable hosting history. The malicious version is registered within days, hosted on a provider with little history, often uses privacy protection at registration, and appears with a link in a message to staff in finance, human resources, or information technology. Judging on the name alone invites false positives, so first sight inside your environment should drive the score.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Recently Registered Lookalike Domain Contacted From the Corporate Network
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: dns
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event.action: query
#   lookalike:
#     query|re: ^(www\.)?(examp1e-corp|exarnple-corp|examplecorp-[a-z0-9]+)\.[a-z]{2,}$
#   new_domain:
#     domain.age_days: < 30
#   filter_owned:
#     domain.owner: example-corp
#   condition: selection and lookalike and new_domain and not filter_owned
# level: high
falsePositives: Marketing campaign and seasonal domains that the brand team registers without telling the security team
Resellers, franchisees, and regional partners that operate approved domains containing the company name
Domain parking and registrar placeholder pages that share a common naming pattern with your brand
Unrelated companies whose names contain the same common word as your brand, registered for legitimate business
Security vendors and researchers that register lookalikes to study or block your brand impersonation
tuningNotes: Keep an authoritative list of domains your organisation owns or authorises, with a named owner and a review date, and filter on that list rather than on registrar text. Tune the similarity match with a strict edit distance and a curated list of homoglyph substitutions, then test it against your own historical alerts before enabling blocking. Require either a certificate issued in the last thirty days or a registration age under thirty days, and prioritise cases where an internal client resolved the name or a user reported the message. The coverage you lose with a strict match is cleverly unrelated names used in text based pretexts, so add reporting from the phishing mailbox and review reported links weekly to catch naming you did not predict.
